There was no bypass pin to be found so after consulting company again we partially pressurized (using reserve brakes and steering switch to power center c1) and taxied to parking. Cause: C HYD PRESS EICASThe bias I had for using the R autopilot was not helpful. I'm uncertain how I missed the information about the R autopilot elevator inop. I know I read everything, it just didn't make it past my eyes into my brain. Suggestions: I need to read intentionally, looking for things I'm wrong about. Carry bypass pins. Keep the SMEs at all costs.
ASRSN:2294322.s: The crew experienced a C HYD PRESS EICAS message on initial climb and incorrectly used the R autopilot due to a missed QRH note about elevator inop. They returned to ZZZZ, landed safely, and taxied using reserve brakes after failing to locate a bypass pin.

ASRSN:2294334.n: During our climb out of ZZZ passing around 28,000 feet we got HYD Y RSVR LO LVL ECAM. We ran the non normal procedure per SOP and completed the ECAM actions and QRH follow ups. We then contacted Dispatch. Dispatch set up a conference call with Maintenance Control and we discussed the failure. It was decided jointly that the best course of action would be to request priority handling and return to ZZZ. Dispatch coordinated with the ZZZ Ops to arrange a tug to bring us from the runway to a gate after we landed. We advised ATC and got direct back to ZZZ. I called the flight attendants and briefed them of the return and precautionary landing back into ZZZ. I then made a PA to let the passengers know we would be returning to ZZZ for a minor hydraulic issue. I let them know they may see safety vehicles after we landed. We set the aircraft up for the return and ran the associated non-normal land app to get the runway distance required for landing. We advised ATC that we would require a tow from the runway and they offered Runway XXR. We slowed the aircraft and configured early and landed the aircraft with no issue. We stopped on the runway. CFR (Crash Fire Rescue) inspected the aircraft after we came to a stop and told us everything looked good and there were no hotspots. I made a PA to the passengers welcoming them back to ZZZ and let them know we would be getting towed back to the gate. I made a few PA's to keep the passengers informed while we waited on the tug to get out to us. When the tug arrived we shut the engines down and they towed us into the gate. At the gate I made a logbook entry and spoke with Maintenance. Had a great crew and FO. Everyone worked together and we handled the situation just like we train. During climb through FL280 for FL330, the crew received an ECAM: HYD Y RSVR LO LVL. The ECAM procedure was accomplished. Following completion of the checklist, the yellow hydraulic reservoir quantity was observed to be completely depleted.The Captain coordinated with Dispatch/Maintenance Control to plan a return to ZZZ. We requested priority handling with ATC, and the flight was cleared direct to ZZZ. Due to loss of nosewheel steering, coordination with ATC was made for a landing on Runway XXR, with arrangements for a tow from the runway after landing.The approach and landing were uneventful. Upon stopping on the runway, airport Fire and Rescue personnel approached the aircraft and conducted an external inspection. After being cleared by emergency services, field operations and maintenance personnel arrived with a tug and towed the aircraft to the gate.I felt ATC and Dispatch/Maintenance Control provided great support throughout the event.
ASRSN:2294334.s: During climb through FL280, the crew received a HYD Y RSVR LO LVL ECAM indicating a depleted yellow hydraulic reservoir. They returned to ZZZ for a precautionary landing on Runway XXR due to lost nosewheel steering, where the aircraft was towed to the gate after a successful external inspection.

ASRSN:2294338.n: CA (me) was PF, FO was PMClimb-out passing through FL280(ish). IMBAL annunciation appeared with an amber fuel quantity on right engine.Left quantity was around 6.8, right quantity was 5.7 and decreasing rapidly.I immediately looked up at the fuel panel. Main wing tank pumps were all on, center tanks were off (no fuel in center), but the crossfeed was on and the blue Valve Open light was on*. I turned the crossfeed valve off immediately and the blue light went out, and we watched the right fuel quantity to see if it would stop decreasing. We discussed that even with the crossfeed valve open and all four pumps on, an imbalance should develop slow, and the fuel quantity should change slower than what we were observing. The right fuel quantity continued dropping rapidly. I asked the FO to open the QRH while we watched for another 3-4 minutes to see if the quantity would slow down. I briefly read the first page of the FUEL LEAK ENGINE checklist quietly and double checked the fuel panel.We were approaching FL370 when I asked the FO to request a turn back to ZZZ. We discussed the nearest field, and we appeared to be halfway between ZZZ and ZZZ1. I elected to return to ZZZ. The left fuel tank was still approximately 6.7, and the right was now down to about 5.0 and still decreasing quicker than the left.ZZZ Center initially gave us a heading of 320 and ask what the nature of our return was. We (FO) answered that it was a possible fuel leak. Center asked if we were requesting priority, and we answered YES. I then told the FO that I was transferring the aircraft to him. He would act as PF, and I would run the QRH.Since the FO had already reviewed some of the QRH quietly, I asked him what page/checklist he was in. He answered that he was in the IMBAL checklist. I found that page, and began officially" running the IMBAL checklist. The engine fuel flows on the 1 & 2 engine were comparable. I decided that a fuel leak was suspected due to the rate at which the fuel quantity was changing. This directed us to run the FUEL LEAK ENGINE checklist. After running the first four steps to verify the fuel panel switch positions (again), we read steps 5 and 6 and did not need to "time" the fuel quantities, as the right changed by >100 pounds per minute (not 500 per 30 minutes as the checklist states). Center gave as an initial descent to FL300(I think) and another vector, followed by direct ZZZ. As we were established in the descent, we both noticed that the fuel leak had significantly slowed or stopped. It made sense to us that with little to no demand on the engine, the fuel leak would slow dramatically.With a fuel leak confirmed, we were in a descent direct to ZZZ. We discussed the decision to shut down the number 2 engine. I decided to leave the engine running at idle at least until we were closer to ZZZ unless we saw additional indications of trouble, and the FO agreed. I paused the FUEL LEAK ENGINE checklist at step XX. (I read the remaining steps but did not accomplish them.)At this point the FO was flying us back to ZZZ, reprogramming the FMS for the arrival, and coordinating with ATC. He briefly answered an ACARS from the dispatcher confirming our return to ZZZ.I began running the non-routine landing considerations checklist. Although the dispatcher was aware we were returning, I advised them of the urgency. I then advised the Flight Attendants of a "Precautionary Landing" and gave the instructions associated with that. I then made a PA to the passengers advising them of our return to ZZZ due to a "fuel issue" and advised them that there would be safety vehicles present.We informed Center that we were requesting RWY XXC and requested ARFF. The FO had loaded the FMS, and I set the ILS frequency and course and reviewed the ILS XXC quietly. I offered the FO the approach and he accepted. FO remained the PF until landing. The weather was VFR and we briefed the visual to XXC. I accomplished theDescent checklist and asked the FAs to prepare the cabin for landing. The FO and I discussed clearing the runway versus stopping on the runway. I decided to stop on the runway to allow room for the ARFF to drive around the wingtips for inspection. We continued to monitor the fuel quantity, and after the Before Landing checklist (to the line), We decided to leave the #2 engine running on the approach, but due to the possibility of a go around (GA), we briefed an Engine out GA. We were watching for and expected the fuel leak to increase again when the throttles came up on approach. I also instructed the FO, that after landing, with the throttles in idle, I would take the aircraft around 60-80 knots and direct him to shutdown Engine 2 as we slowed to a stop.The FO did a textbook approach and landing. I took the aircraft at 70 knots and he cutoff the number 2 engine.ARFF stated that they only saw drips of fluid near the landing gear and nothing significant. The fuel quantity did not change after we shut down the number 2 engine. We called Ops to get a gate, and ARFF followed us back to the gate uneventfully. The fuel was approximately 6.0 on the left and 4.3 on the right side.* Side note*. We had just flown this aircraft on a ZZZZ turn, and landed in ZZZ with 2 write-ups. (1) Engine 2 oil needed servicing, and (2) LEFT PACK light illumined. We were the ones that ran the shutdown checklist. We left the airplane to go through customs, back through TSA, and returned to the aircraft. We accomplished the preflight and ran the Before Start Checklist. I remember the crossfeed valve being closed. I do not remember it being open at any point prior to the event. Either it was done while we left the airplane to go through customs (and we missed it on the preflight), or I unintentionally bumped or moved it at some point. I do not believe the crossfeed valve was the culprit given the fuel rate continued several minutes after the valve was closed and only slowed/stopped when the engines were at idle.Cause: Possible engine fuel leak."
ASRSN:2294338.s: The Captain and First Officer experienced a rapid right fuel imbalance during climb-out, suspecting an engine fuel leak despite closing the crossfeed valve. They returned to ZZZ, landed safely with the right engine running, and shut it down on the runway after ARFF inspection found only minor drips.

ASRSN:2294383.n: Pack 2 was MEL'd in ZZZ prior to flight to ZZZ1. Reaching altitude, FL240, we encountered icing, followed by a Wing A/I fail and master warning because we were in icing conditions. We attempted to go out of icing, then we noticed our cabin pressure altitude start to climb above 10000ft, at which we declared an emergency and diverted to ZZZ2. Our O2 masks that we donned in the flight deck were dry rotted as well, providing an additional safety concern. Normal approach to landing and under max landing weight. No trucks requested and no pax concerns.Suggestion: All O2 masks be inspected immediately fleetwide. Improved onboard weather detection is required fleetwide. Aircraft X. ZZZ TO ZZZ1. Prior to departure from ZZZ, maintenance was contacted and MEL 21-XX-X was added for a PACK 2 failure/leak. Normal taxi, takeoff and departure with a normal climb out to 24000ft. At cruise, we encountered light rime icing. We received a wing anti-ice failure followed by anti-ice inop warning. We requested a descent with ATC. During the descent, we experienced an increase in cabin pressure altitude into the amber, then red range. We donned our oxygen masks, but they did not seal properly. Per maintenance, the internal tubing was dry rotted and leaking. We requested priority handling with ATC, squawked XXXX, and increased the rate of descent to 4000 ft./min. down to 10,000 feet. At 10,000 feet, we dumped the cabin pressure. We coordinated with ATC to divert to ZZZ2. We did not require special assistance or emergency vehicles at ZZZ2. We performed a normal approach to normal landing, gross weight was under Max landing weight. We arrived at the gate normally. The FA reported no abnormalities in the cabin and no passenger complaints. The aircraft was handed off to maintenance in ZZZ2.Cause: Systems failure, Maintenance inspection failure, Limited weather detection capabilities.Suggestion: Inspect all crew oxygen masks immediately fleetwide for proper operation. Install improved on board weather detection systems Fleet wide. No change to routing occurred with dispatch after MEL was added to release. This suggests limited weather detection capabilities for both air crew and dispatch.
ASRSN:2294383.s: Flight crew on Aircraft X encountered icing at FL240, causing wing anti-ice failure and a cabin pressure loss due to dry-rotted oxygen masks. The crew declared an emergency, diverted to ZZZ2, and landed safely, attributing the incident to maintenance and weather detection failures.

ASRSN:2294421.n: Girt bar was not in the slide cover brackets but door streamer was left across door 1R.
ASRSN:2294421.s: The reporter observed that the girt bar was not secured in the slide cover brackets, while the door streamer remained across door 1R. No specific aircraft, phase of flight, or outcome was described in the narrative.

ASRSN:2294544.n: Flight attendants disarmed & cross SOP. The 1L door was disarmed & crosschecked, the girt bar was secured with tension. When the gate agent opened the door, the girt bar became loose & started to fall out of the left bracket. Both fwd flight attendants noticed & immediately made it known that the gate agent needed to stop. The gate agent stopped, the girt bar was secured once again & we deplaned as normal.
ASRSN:2294544.s: Flight attendants reported that while disarming the 1L door, the girt bar became loose and fell from its bracket when the gate agent opened the door. The attendants stopped the agent, re-secured the bar, and the flight deplaned normally.

ASRSN:2294619.n: I'm FA A. Upon arrival made the call to verify and disarm. I monitored and cross checked then realized no one was at the jetbridge as we were about 25 min early. Instead making the all call to verify the doors were verified and disarmed, I put my girtbar back in the lock thinking one door had to remain armed until I saw the jetbridge moving. Passengers were ready to get out and I held them back saying it would be just a minute. The gate agent knocked on the door before I rerepeated monitor and challenge. I gave the thumbs up in error. Accidental slide deployment.
ASRSN:2294619.s: Flight Attendant A accidentally deployed a slide upon arrival while 25 minutes early and before jetbridge connection. The error occurred when the attendant incorrectly gave a thumbs-up signal during the door verification process, causing the slide to deploy while passengers were held back.

ASRSN:2294620.n: We parked at the gate, the bell went off I got up, FA A said verify and disarm doors, I proceeded to verify and disarm my door. I was confused why the FA A wasn't immediately disarming the door. I heard FA A say I need to wait to disarm cause the gate agent wasn't there, I mentioned that I see the jet bridge and he told me that there was a thing in the procedure where you don't disarm the door until the jet bridge was there, I mentioned that the jet bridge was there, I saw him get down on the ground and saw him take the girt bar out, I assumed he was disarming the door, I turned around to re verify that my door was disarmed and heard a noise and turned around and saw the door open with the gate agent standing there and the slide was dropped out of the bussel slightly. The gate agent looked shocked and proceeded to call someone and the FA A called the other flight attendants and the captain informing me on what happened.
ASRSN:2294620.s: A flight attendant reported that after parking, a colleague delayed disarming the door until the gate agent arrived, causing the slide to partially deploy when the door opened. The incident occurred because the crew member misunderstood the procedure regarding jet bridge presence and door disarm timing.

ASRSN:2294631.n: I was holding the X and the other wingwalker went to drop the towbar after confirming with the driver that brakes were set. When the towbar was dropped the plane began to move forward a few seconds later after the pushback began to pull back.Cause: The pilot released brakes earlyI got the pilots attention and got him to reset brakes.I don't know what happened but the pilot seemed distracted because he wasn't looking at me holding the X. I said to pilot 'Parking Brakes Set.'He responded 'Brakes Set.'I gave hand signal to wing walkers.Wing walker disconnected tow bar and plane began moving forward.Cause: Pilot did not set brakes.Pilot side wingwalker got pilots attention and got him to set brakes.I recall pilots talking to each other, but don't know what happened on their end.
ASRSN:2294631.s: During pushback, the aircraft moved forward after the towbar was disconnected because the pilot released the brakes early and was distracted. A wingwalker alerted the pilot, who then reset the parking brakes to stop the movement.

ASRSN:2294641.n: On that date we were working flight ABCD. The following statement is to the best of my recollection and after reviewing the video. The incident occurred a week ago, when we pushed out the flight and disconnected the tow bar, from the aircraft. I was on the right wing and was tasked with the actual disconnection of the tow bar. Person A was the driver and was on the headset in communication with the pilot. Person B was on the left wing and was tasked with notifying the pilot when all was clear. Person A pushed out the aircraft to the alley and came to a stop. Once he was stopped I walked over to the tow bar and began lowering the landing gear on the tow bar but leaving the wheels off the ground about an inch or so. I leave the wheels off the ground so that I don't create tension and/or possibly to cause damage to the equipment or aircraft in case of any movement. Once I lowered the wheels I looked and Person A to give me the brakes set signal. I then returned signal. I then proceed to disconnect the headset cord and the towbar. Right before I lift the handle to release the tow bar I normally look at the light and see if it is on. Meaning the brakes have been set. I am not 100 percent sure as this happened a week ago. I do remember lifting the handle and seeing the tow bar dropping to the latch that holds the tow bar in place. After the drop Person A reversed about a foot and stopped I noticed the plane start to roll forward. I motioned to Person A to move out of the way to reverse as the plane was moving towards the push out tractor and tow bar. He did reverse about 10 ft and stopped. I signaled to Person B to notify the pilot so set brakes to which he did. Seeing the plane was not stopping I signaled to Person A to move out of the way and clear the area as to not create any damage or possibly get injured. Person B was furiously trying to get the pilot's attention, but the pilot was not paying attention to the situation. Person B was even jumping up and down waving his wands. I noticed Person A was clear and out of the way and since the pilot was not responding to Person B I then carefully without getting ran over by the plane I tapped the fuselage and then a few seconds and about 20ft later the plane came to a stop. I then proceeded to disconnect the bypass pin and walk it over to Person B. Person B showed the pin and I believe saluted him. I then proceeded to calm Person B down as we were lucky that our quick thinking adverted a possible aircraft damage or worse possibility of an injury to a passenger, flight crew or coworker.I'm not sure why it happened. Person A said that he gave the command to set brakes and pilot said they were set. I do know that after the event it seemed the pilot was distracted. Maybe he accidentally released the brakes. The reason I say he was distracted was because Person B was trying to get his attention and he did not react or responded by setting the brakes right away. It wasn't til I believe I tapped on the fuselage that he reacted.As mentioned above. I quickly motioned for Person A to move out of the way. And signaled for Person B to get the pilot to set brakes. I believe after I tapped on the plane is when he realized what was going on. Once he set them. He did not call to return to gate or anything. Nor did he call ops. He taxi out and left.Suggestions: Honestly, I guess double confirmation on brakes being set from push back operator and pilot. Also while disconnecting tow bar pilots have to remain aware of ground crew and not distracted.
ASRSN:2294641.s: During pushback of flight ABCD, the aircraft rolled forward after towbar disconnection because the pilot failed to set brakes despite ground crew signals. The reporter prevented damage by tapping the fuselage to alert the distracted pilot, who then stopped the aircraft and taxied out without reporting the incident.

ASRSN:2294642.n: AIRCRAFT X - So event started as aircraft arrived at XA:45 and inbound crew didn't report bird strikes inbound. Outbound crew reported finding a radome hit on preflight walk around around XB:00/XC:15 and techs were sent out and notified CC (Crew Chief) @ XD:40 that both engines had evidence of bird ingestion in both engines aircraft put in AOS (Aircraft out of Service) status @ XE:45. Notified by management that they will notify us if aircraft will be given to a hanger crew or if we will work it so CC removed techs off aircraft pending managements directive. notified around XF:00 prior to management crew brief that we will stay assigned to Aircraft X. Meeting lasted till XG:45 and crew was sent out to aircraft but we were not notified aircraft was moved to fence X so techs went to fence X to continue with initial bird strike inspection and start working managements previous directive of ( Aircraft checks and inbounds) 3 people were assigned initially and 6 more were assigned to another aircraft but once finished with other aircraft they went over to Aircraft X @ fence X was approached by management to look at the engines and verify/ confirm the bird strike ingestion. Due to managements request of updating apc with techs assignments on every item and task given verbally last week by same management on shift CC was not able to leave desk till XH:45. arrived at A/C as well as manager Person A. Who immediately was irate at the progress giving questions that I just arrived to confirm. We approached the aircraft as Person A was asking where are the bird strikes to where this is the first time CC witness's the engines in question and upon initial look verified immediately bird strike on root of fan blade and residue in booster stage agreed upon with Person A . While heading to #2 engine Person A was asking questions in a loud irate/angered manner regarding why techs are taking long why are the engines not butterflied and explained a/c was moved our meeting took long and figuring out with inspection what card they used as this is the crews 1st 737 core ingestion requiring borescope. Asking why no a/c cart or hose was used while plane was at the gate and explained again about the misunderstanding by management and a/c move and meeting. at XI:05 techs mentioned they were heading to the other side to take their lunch period closed up the aircraft per Procedures Manual as 737 does not have auto fire suppression and tsa policy req's the aircraft not be left unattended with stairs. During the XJ:30 production meeting Person A was hostile on the update on Aircraft X explaining that why the techs left at XH:00 and that they were ' on his time' I did not acknowledge that statement . Pressure to rush work increased after the call with constant request for updates and @ XK:15 was informed inspection arrived and questioned the workcard given to them that they can work off the AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual) quicker to expedite the inspection and the mechanics confirmed with CC and I updated Person B as he was next to memore pressure was added as management changed their mind extended the etr (Estimated Time of Repair) to XL:00 and requested all items found during the transit check ( 3 MWA and 2 nose tires and several interior items) be fixed which crew chief had informed his 7 mechs about the update as management requested 2 stay back to work the wake up checklist on Aircraft Y and finish up their paperwork on Aircraft Z. This seemed retaliatory but the constant interruptions and changes are causing confusion / pressure / stress and uneeded hostility due to micro management coming from above. F crew is set up for failure with managements expectation of obtaining 8.5 hours of RON (Routine Overnight) work out of them when last bird out and first birds in @XK:00. Managements constant push harassment threats towards performance counseling's when they only allow for very little set up time or account for movement between aircraft / tooling isadding stress and pressure let alone the constant bird dogging or second guessing is interrupting mechanics and presents a safety risk let alone violation of company code of conduct with constant hostile / verbal abuse toward several CC's on meetings. The growing pains of the station are to much now time isnt being properly tracked on inbound items in safe and those hours are not applied to work accomplished management is pushing more work than manpower is available threatening by way of punitive discipline as several crew chiefs have submitted reports and ethics complaints. Safety should always be priority as company's constant speech and read and signs. Cause: dictating maintenance / micro managing / pressure / lack of knowledge on part of management on proper time management and to high of expectations without consideration for safety only production metrics . Suggestions: management be retrained with leadership course in ZZZ and re review of company code of conduct as well as critical behaviors and for accountability and company standards be followed not ignored for production metric goals
ASRSN:2294642.s: Mechanics and Crew Chiefs inspected Aircraft X for bird strikes after management moved the aircraft and issued conflicting directives. The reporter attributed the resulting safety risks and stress to management's hostile micromanagement, unrealistic production expectations, and lack of maintenance knowledge.

ASRSN:2294662.n: I was on approach to runway 30 at KHAF, one traffic was in the pattern 30 so I let them go first and lined up as number 2 for landing which I clearly announced on the CTAF 122.8. The previous traffic had no issue performing a touch and go on runway 30. There were 2 other planes holding short 30 and another aircraft inbound for runway 30. I then announced a 2 nm final. The other plane (Aircraft Y) was on an IFR flight plan and announced it holding short runway 12. Roughly 10 seconds later Aircraft Y asked if anyone is approaching 30, the inbound aircraft said they were on a 7.5NM final and before I had the chance of saying something they [Aircraft Y] were lining up and saying that they are taking off. The plane holding short 30 mentioned that I, Aircraft X, was on short final, I even had the recognition lights on for easier detection. Aircraft Y decided to continue forcing me into a go around which causes my G1000 to spike for a second telling me that there is traffic.
ASRSN:2294662.s: The pilot of Aircraft X on short final to runway 30 at KHAF was forced to go around when Aircraft Y, holding short of runway 12, initiated takeoff despite traffic advisories. This conflict caused Aircraft X's G1000 traffic alert to spike, though no collision occurred.

ASRSN:2294676.n: I supplied an aircraft which had been through a condition inspection X days prior to use for a 709 check ride. FAA personnel from the ZZZ FSDO reviewed the aircraft for suitability for said check ride. The A&P inspectors stated they were not impressed with the condition of the wooden propeller on the aircraft but it was 'experimental' so they were unable to ground the aircraft but recommended to the flight examiner that he may not want to choose to fly in the plane. He stated on the telephone with another safety compliance officer in ZZZ that the 'magic words' never were said to me and the exam had not begun. The 709 checkride examiner decided to agree with the other inspectors and declined to give me the check ride. I received a letter from the FSDO stating that I had to surrender my license and that the checkride was 'unsatisfactory' I have since sent the propeller to the manufacturer who states there was no threat of an issue flying the prop and he is refinishing and returning the propeller for a nominal charge.
ASRSN:2294676.s: FAA inspectors and a checkride examiner declined a 709 checkride for an experimental aircraft due to concerns over its wooden propeller condition. The examiner marked the ride unsatisfactory and required license surrender, though the manufacturer later confirmed the propeller posed no flight safety threat.

ASRSN:2294686.n: While on a straight in final about 3 miles out for Runway 30 at Merced (MCE), another aircraft called 'turning base' and turned right in front of me. I went around immediately and offset to the right side of the runway so I could keep them in sight and stay clear.After the go around, I told traffic on CTAF that I was extending my upwind. I stayed on upwind longer than usual and climbed to about 400 feet above pattern altitude because the other pilot hadn't been responding to any of my calls and I wasn't sure what they were going to do next.On my MFD I saw them departing and climbing behind me at roughly my same altitude, and it looked like they were converging on me. To stay clear I turned right and started descending. While I was maneuvering, I realized the Class D airspace northeast of Merced was nearby. I double checked my position on the MFD, made sure I was below and clear of her, then turned left to stay away from the Delta boundary. It's possible I briefly touched the edge of that airspace while avoiding them.I realize how important it is to stay flexible, communicate clearly, and maintain full awareness of traffic and nearby airspace, especially when I notice that another pilot isn't following normal pattern procedures.
ASRSN:2294686.s: A pilot on final for Runway 30 at Merced executed a go-around after another aircraft turned right in front, then maneuvered to avoid a converging conflict while climbing to 400 feet above pattern altitude. The pilot likely briefly entered Class D airspace while descending and turning to maintain separation from the unresponsive traffic.

ASRSN:2294694.n: Departed ZZZ airport northwest-bound toward ZZZ1 airport. My intended route was to fly a 320 heading for a few miles and then turn westbound toward ZZZ1. During my takeoff roll I heard ZZZ tower clear a state trooper helicopter to depart from a taxiway northwest-bound. I made note that this was the same direction as my route. At approximately 5nm from ZZZ2, I was cleared to change frequencies. A few moments later I wanted to turn westbound toward ZZZ1, but I noticed on my TCAS that there was traffic in close proximity at the same altitude. I looked over my shoulder, but did not see any traffic. The helicopter was most likely obscured by the wing. I began a turn toward the west, but immediately got a traffic alert and stopped the turn. I could now see the helicopter and I turned to a heading which roughly paralleled their track. It appeared that the helicopter was attempting to overtake me. Soon after, the helicopter climbed above me. Once they were greater than 500ft above me according to TCAS, I resumed my turn toward the west. The flight concluded without incident. It would have been prudent for ZZZ Tower to advise one or both of us of the potential conflict. Particularly the helicopter as they were the faster of the two and likely to overtake.
ASRSN:2294694.s: A pilot departing ZZZ airport northwest-bound encountered a state trooper helicopter cleared on a similar track, resulting in a TCAS traffic alert during a westbound turn. The pilot aborted the turn to avoid the overtaking helicopter, which climbed 500 feet above, concluding the flight safely while noting a lack of tower conflict advisories.

ASRSN:2294698.n: While on a practice RNAV Rwy 11 approach to GIF (Winter Haven, FL) an aircraft appeared on my ADS-B in screen. It was at my altitude and heading directly for me. I took evasive action, including turning and descending. The aircraft turned and descended to continue to head straight towards me. It then disappeared from my screen, at which point I held altitude and heading until it reappeared. I then made visual contact. It passed 200' below me and less then 200' horizontal to me. It appeared to heading directly towards LAL (Lakeland).
ASRSN:2294698.s: A pilot conducting a practice RNAV Rwy 11 approach to GIF observed an aircraft on ADS-B In at the same altitude heading directly toward them. After evasive maneuvers, the pilot visually confirmed the other aircraft passed within 200 feet vertically and horizontally while heading toward LAL.

ASRSN:2294711.n: Our destination JPX is an uncontrolled airport (part-time control tower in the Summer season only). The winds were light but just slightly favored runway 10, and this is what runway we requested due to the short runway length there.Our aircraft was a few miles east of the FOK Class D airspace at 3000ft. We were being vectored towards MATHW waypoint for the RNAV Z Runway 10 approach. The ATC frequency was very busy, and I observed numerous TCAS targets on my MFD (Multi-function Flight Display) in the area around and below us. The aircraft that caused the conflict in this episode was approximately 5 miles in front of me, between my 12 and 1 o'clock position at 2500 ft when the controller instructed us to turn right direct to MATHW, and very shortly thereafter cleared us to descend to 2000 ft. I had some concern about that target, but the frequency was too congested for us to question the course/intentions of that target. Just as I was starting my descent, this target started to climb and appeared to be moving toward our airplane, causing an immediate RA command for us to climb, and we complied without delay. The TCAS was instrumental in helping to prevent a collision, because: 1)I never visually acquired the target, and 2) It was at least 5 seconds before the controller could issue deconflicting instructions due to frequency congestion.Ultimately, we were instructed to return to 4000 feet and vectored northwest away from the cluster of traffic in the space between our airplane and the destination airport. Subsequently, when the frequency congestion cleared up a bit, the controller suggested vectors to the opposite runway, as he was observing that other VFR airplanes appeared to be maneuvering for that runway. This would have been more useful for us to know earlier in the arrival, but again, just too much traffic and frequency congestion in the area for the PNF to be off frequency for any period of time to sort out what seemed to be a very fluid situation at the uncontrolled destination airport.I think it relevant to add I was astounded by the density of traffic in the proximity of our destination this day. I have flown passengers commercially for 20 years and cannot recall seeing this level of density and traffic mix (small GA, helicopter, and jet traffic) at an uncontrolled airport simultaneously. The overlying airspace is Class E with no regulatory requirement for VFR traffic to be in direct communication with ATC. I have flown in Class C or TRSA areas with less traffic than was operating over the eastern portion of Long Island, NY today. It also strains belief that JPX only operates a control tower during Summer months, today there absolutely was enough traffic at this field and in the immediate surrounding airspace to warrant a local control tower.
ASRSN:2294711.s: A commercial jet crew encountered a TCAS Resolution Advisory while descending toward uncontrolled airport JPX due to a conflicting aircraft climbing into their path. The collision was avoided by the TCAS, as frequency congestion prevented the controller from issuing timely deconflicting instructions.

ASRSN:2294712.n: A training flight was conducted under VMC conditions on Day 0 in a Super Decathlon with a private pilot acting as PIC in the front seat and CFI in the back seat. The flight departed just after XA:00 local time from ZZZ, leaving the pattern to the south to conduct simulated emergencies and simulated off field landings. Approximately 10 minutes into the flight while turning right base to final at approximately 1200' AGL for a chosen farm field to make a simulated landing, a yellow Cub was seen at the 10 or 11 o'clock position 100'-200' away and ~20 feet below the Super Decathlon. The Cub appeared to be in a left bank and moving away from the Super Decathlon. The pilot of the Super Decathlon noted the close traffic over intercom, increased power to full throttle, and increased the rate of right bank in order to avoid the Cub. Due to the poor visibility from the backseat and the immediate increase in bank angle hiding the Cub from view under the belly of the Super Decathlon, the CFI did not make visual contact with the Cub at any point. After moving away from the point of near miss, the Super Decathlon climbed to a higher altitude and left the area to continue the flight without issue.Shortly prior to departing ZZZ, a yellow Cub has been observed departing the field and leaving the pattern without making any traffic calls on CTAF. The CFI had been observing ADS-B traffic on an EFB in the plane sporadically during the flight, but did not observe the Cub at any point on ForeFlight. It is hypothesized that the Cub, not having had an electrical system at the time of its construction, may not have had accommodations for COMM radio or ADS-B.The PIC in the front seat of the Super Decathlon lost situational awareness and failed to clear for traffic while focused on the simulated engine out. Due to the tandem seating of the Super Decathlon obstructing the view of the CFI in the back seat, extra care should be taken to clear for traffic before maneuvers. Task saturation and tunnel vision were also contributing factors.It is possible that the view of the Cub was obstructed by the cowl of the Super Decathlon for most of the maneuver, contributing to the failure of the Super Decathlon pilot to see and avoid. The high wing Cub may have been unaware of the presence of the Super Decathlon entirely due to its configuration and the fact that the Super Decathlon was approaching the Cub from behind and above.Flight following was not obtained at any time during the flight. At the time of the event, the Super Decathlon was monitoring the CTAF frequency for ZZZ. Flight following may have added to situational awareness in the Super Decathlon.No communications were exchanged between either aircraft during or after the event, and the tail number of the Cub is unknown.
ASRSN:2294712.s: During a training flight in a Super Decathlon, the PIC and CFI experienced a near miss with a yellow Cub while turning base to final at 1200' AGL. The incident resulted from the PIC's loss of situational awareness during a simulated emergency, compounded by the Cub's lack of radio/ADS-B and obstructed views from the tandem seating.

ASRSN:2294713.n: While on an instrument flight plan from S43 to ZZZ with a coworker we decided to return to S43 through RNT. We were on the RNAV GPS 34 into RNT and got cleared in then sent to the CTAF at around 1600ft MSL. Upon switching frequencies and calling our final we heard a helicopter in the downwind call to tell us they would follow us in. There was also a Pilatus PC-12 at the hold short waiting for the landing traffic. They alerted us they had a 4 minute clearance time so I wanted to make sure to get off the runway as soon as possible for them. Upon landing I exited to the west side of the runway on A5 and began taxiing back toward runway 34 so that we could file our new IFR flight plan. The clouds that were to the north prevented us from flying VFR back to our destination of S43. As soon as we taxied back toward the runway we heard a call from the helicopter saying 'thanks for cutting me off on final' and we saw them about 100ft above us over taxiway A. I apologized over the radio then we proceed to file our flight plan, get our clearance and depart. Someone called the facility we rented the aircraft from to complain and that is how I heard there may be an issue. I looked at the right of way rules and could not determine if either aircraft was directly at fault. This report is being submitted because I am unsure of who is at fault but wanted to alert the authorities of the incident.
ASRSN:2294713.s: The pilot reported a near-midair conflict with a helicopter while taxiing on runway 34 at RNT after landing. The helicopter pilot accused the fixed-wing aircraft of cutting them off on final, though the reporter could not determine fault under right-of-way rules.

ASRSN:2294719.n: Helicopter stopped reporting on CTAF in the lake after making only a couple of reports entering the lake/seaplane base environment. I started my takeoff to the south and the helicopter came past me on my right, on the west side of the lake. I didn't see them until I was established in the climb. I continued to climb straight ahead due to terrain to my east and the helicopter to the west, which was now slightly ahead and to my right. Approaching the south end of the lake I asked what the helicopter's intentions were as they started to climb into my path of travel, I initiated a hard climbing right turn to avoid and pass behind the helicopter who continued straight on their course towards the waterfront. When I began my turn, I was still low relative to the terrain on the eastside of the lake and it was too risky to turn left due to the wind velocity and rising terrain.
ASRSN:2294719.s: A pilot taking off south from a seaplane base encountered a helicopter that had stopped reporting on CTAF and was climbing into their path. The pilot executed a hard climbing right turn to avoid the helicopter, as turning left was too risky due to rising terrain and wind velocity.

ASRSN:2294723.n: While I was taxiing back to Runway XX a jet that landed ahead of me on XX said I landed on an active runway.When I landed I did not see him on the runway. When I turned off the runway and was clear of the Runway XX I announced it on the radio, I looked both ways for taxiway traffic, and proceeded to then turn onto the taxiway back to Runway XX. I then received the call on the radio asking me for my tail #. The person on the radio asked me if I landed on an active runway. I responded that I did not see any plane on the runway when I landed. I do not believe I landed on an active runway.
ASRSN:2294723.s: A pilot reported a runway incursion concern while taxiing back to Runway XX after landing, triggered by a radio call from a jet that had landed ahead. The pilot stated they did not see the other aircraft on the runway during their landing and denied landing on an active runway.

ASRSN:2294724.n: Events occured at s27, an untowered airport with moderate traffic during peak hours of the day. Training Aircraft X from s27 with student pilot and CFI onboard was flying the left downwind for runway 31. Aircraft Y contacted CTAF freq and announced they would be back taxiing on runway 31. Aircraft X turned left base for 31, and Aircraft Y cleared the runway. Aircraft X turned onto final and completed a touch and go without incident, announcing on CTAF that we would remain in left traffic for runway 31. Aircraft Y departed while Aircraft X was on the upwind from runway 31. Aircraft X turned onto left crosswind approx 1.5 nm from departure end of runway 31. Aircraft Y began nonstandard 45 degree left crosswind around 0.5 nm from departure end of runway 31. Aircraft X turned left crosswind to left downwind while Aircraft Y continued outbound on nonstandard left crosswind, bringing the Aircraft X and Aircraft Y into conflict. Aircraft Y announced that he would not be a factor for the traffic in the downwind, unknown if he had visual contact with Aircraft X. Aircraft X established visual contact with Aircraft Y, who was crossing left to right approximately 300 ft off the nose of the Aircraft X at same altitude. Aircraft X contacted Aircraft Y and advised of the conflict, and requested he fly standard pattern in the future. Aircraft Y departed area to the west.it is the opinion of the writer that the Aircraft Y pilot demonstrated the hazardous attitudes of impulsivity, macho, and anti-authority. first issue was back taxiing on an active runway with traffic in the pattern, potentially creating a conflict with landing traffic when a taxiway was available and empty. second issue was Aircraft Y pilot departing immediately following slower traffic, and seeming in a rush to exit the traffic pattern, deciding to turn an early crosswind and cutting off traffic on the downwind instead of flying the upwind and then departing on the crosswind.
ASRSN:2294724.s: A student pilot and CFI in Aircraft X encountered a conflict with Aircraft Y at untowered airport S27 while flying left traffic for Runway 31. The reporter attributes the incident to Aircraft Y's hazardous attitudes, citing its back-taxiing on an active runway and nonstandard early crosswind turn that cut off Aircraft X.

ASRSN:2294725.n: During a VFR personal flight, I was descending to a lower altitude but unintentionally went lower than intended, reaching approximately 700 feet AGL over a populated area instead of maintaining the required 1,000 feet. I was attempting to fly lower for better visibility and scenery, but I misjudged my altitude and briefly descended beyond what was appropriate. This was a mistake on my part, not due to distraction or outside factors.Once I recognized the deviation, I immediately corrected back to a safe altitude and ensured full compliance for the remainder of the flight. This incident reinforced the importance of strict altitude monitoring, especially when operating near towns, and I will apply more frequent altitude cross-checks in the future.
ASRSN:2294725.s: During a VFR personal flight, the pilot unintentionally descended to 700 feet AGL over a populated area instead of maintaining the required 1,000 feet due to misjudging altitude for better visibility. The pilot immediately corrected to a safe altitude, attributing the error to personal mistake rather than distraction.

ASRSN:2294728.n: While parked on the ramp, I received my taxi clearance from BIS Ground: 'Taxi to Runway 13 via Charlie.' No specific routing instructions were given to reach Taxiway C, which is common. As I began taxiing from the ramp under that clearance, I noticed a stop sign positioned near what appeared to be a newly surfaced taxiway (A2), along with a sign instructing ground vehicles to contact ATC before crossing.Since I had a valid taxi clearance, had not received any instructions to avoid that route, and there were no NOTAMs or advisories indicating that Taxiway A2 was closed, I believed it was acceptable to use A2 to transition to Taxiway C. The signage seemed intended for airport maintenance vehicles rather than aircraft and the pavement looked as if it was ready for use.After crossing A2, Ground Control advised that Taxiway A2 was not currently in use due to recent resurfacing. I acknowledged, apologized for the misunderstanding, and continued as instructed. Shortly after, I received takeoff clearance and departed without further issue.In hindsight, I should have contacted Ground for clarification before crossing the stop sign. I believe the primary contributing factor was a lack of mutual communication with ground control, lack of advisory's/notice's with the repavement, and lack of situational clarity on my end. Specific routing instructions, an advisory regarding A2's recent closure, or me inquiring about the area before crossing would have prevented the confusion.Going forward, I will verify any ambiguous signage or unclear taxi routes with Ground Control before proceeding. I have also scheduled additional instruction to refresh my knowledge of airport surface operations and signage interpretation.I'm writing this as both a reflection and a reminder to other pilots: when in doubt--ask. If something feels uncertain, clarification is the safest and most professional option. That's exactly what I will do next time I am faced with a similar situation.
ASRSN:2294728.s: The pilot, while taxiing from the ramp to Runway 13, crossed a stop sign on newly resurfaced Taxiway A2 believing it was open. Ground Control later advised the taxiway was closed due to resurfacing, an outcome the pilot attributed to a lack of specific routing instructions, advisories, and mutual communication.

ASRSN:2294762.n: Student and I departed airport for local training flight for multiengine add on. While flying above 4500ft msl we were practicing procedure to shut down, troubleshoot, secure, and air restart an engine. While completing air restart checklist, engine did not come back to life. We decided to completely secure engine and proceed back to the home airport. Able to maintain headings and altitudes with atc and picked up a pop up IFR clearance back into destination while being single engine. Did the ILS XX at ZZZ while being with ATC and tower without declaring an emergency. We used crew resource management to make sure all checklists were completed and briefed what we would do if second engine failed also. Looking back declaring an emergency is something we should have done that we failed to use. After landing we were able to exit the runway and get the left engine back to running for taxi.
ASRSN:2294762.s: A student and instructor conducting multiengine training experienced an engine failure above 4500ft MSL during a restart attempt. They returned single-engine under IFR without declaring an emergency, landed safely, and later restarted the engine for taxi.

ASRSN:2294775.n: Runway Excursion After Tire Failure on Landing Roll -- Mooney M20JDuring the landing rollout in a Mooney, the aircraft suddenly pulled sharply to the left. I applied right rudder and regained runway alignment briefly, but the aircraft began pulling left again despite full right rudder and right brake application. The left main tire had failed, later determined to likely be caused by foreign object damage (FOD). The aircraft departed the left side of runway XX, and the left wing contacted a taxiway sign, resulting in skin damage.One passenger was on board, no injuries occurred. After the aircraft came to a stop, I secured it, notified airport operations, and coordinated for a tug to move it to the ramp/hangar area. Right wind from 030 10 gusting 15 was also a contributing factor. Tire failure during landing rollout, likely from FOD. Loss of directional control following tire failure.Suggestions: Review of directional control procedures and emergency response for landing gear/tire failures.
ASRSN:2294775.s: The pilot of a Mooney M20J with one passenger experienced a left main tire failure likely caused by FOD during landing rollout, exacerbated by gusty right winds. This resulted in a loss of directional control, a runway excursion, and left wing skin damage after contacting a taxiway sign, though no injuries occurred.

ASRSN:2294783.n: We were on base leg to RW13L descending out of 3000' to 2000', as we reached 2700' we received a RA with an aircraft 400' below us. The pilot flying immediately responded to RA and avoided the other aircraft. We assumed the aircraft must have taken off of ADS and was climbing out. Once we were clear of the aircraft we radioed the controller and advised of the deviation. We were questioned 'were there any injuries?' to which we replied no. At that point we were vectored to the final approach course and cleared for the approach.
ASRSN:2294783.s: The flight crew on base leg to RW13L received a Resolution Advisory at 2700' for an aircraft 400' below, likely climbing from ADS. The pilot flying executed the RA to avoid the conflict, reported no injuries, and was subsequently vectored for the approach.

ASRSN:2294787.n: I was the PIC for a ZZZZ to PASC Part 91 repositioning leg.I filed an IFR flight plan to PASC at 10,000' via THAWD, with a plan for the block 10,000'-12,000' if needed to avoid prolonged icing on our planned route. The NWS AAWU (Alaska Aviation Weather Unit) icing forecast indicated isolated moderate icing over the White Mountains and Yukon Flats from the altitudes 030-120 during our flight.We started to pick up ice at 8,000' (light mixed).On the climb to 10,000' I realized that wouldn't keep us from continuous icing conditions, asked/received for block 10,000'-12,000'.At 12,000' icing persisted (moderate mixed)...asked/received block 10,000'-14,000'.Icing increased.Increased power to maximum Torque/ITT (Interstage Turbine Temperature) to maintain airspeed above icing limits.At 13,300' unable positive climb within icing airspeed limits, started shallow (200 fpm) descent to maintain icing airspeed.Stall buffet began, airspeed dropped below icing limits.Increased descent to 600fpm, no result, then 1000fpm, no result, 2000fpm halted airspeed degradation.Descended through clearance limit (10,000'), received several lower altitudes from ATC...all unable. I believe the controller said MSA was 4,000' in our immediate area.Found MEF (Maximum Elevation Figure) on the VFR charts (1,500'), made the decision that it would be the absolute floor.VMC began around 8,000'.Stall buffet ended around 4,000'.Leveled off at MEF (+7C SAT) still covered in ice...it took roughly 5 minutes for ice to fully shed from aircraft.Started shallow climb to safer altitudes...maintained VMC rest of journey.Notable additions:Unfortunately, in the descent, we continued to aggressively pick ice until approximately 8,000'...an estimated 1' had accumulated on all unprotected surfaces, to include inside engine intakes.Turning around was not a viable/safe option once buffet set in.I did not knowingly fly into severe icing...once realized, I reacted accordingly.For the entire event, all de-ice/anti-ice systems were operational and in use.ATC communications and instrument flight rules during this event were limited to the extent to meet the situation.After this event, ATC issued a CWA (Center Weather Advisory) for severe icing.
ASRSN:2294787.s: The PIC of a Part 91 flight encountered persistent moderate mixed icing while climbing from 8,000' to 14,000', causing stall buffet and airspeed loss despite maximum power and de-ice systems. The crew descended below their clearance limit to 1,500' to shed accumulated ice and regain control before continuing in VMC.

ASRSN:2294794.n: IFR Low Altitude Charts and VFR Sectionals Do Not Have the Same Name for Many Airports.This is an ongoing danger and needs to be addressed! The 'Memorial Names' need to be removed from the airport data blocks and the commonly used names inserted on IFR and VFR sectionals. It will also reduce clutter on the sectionals. e.g. Referring to the charts for the Jackson, MS area, MBO is labeled 'Bruce Campbell Field' on one chart and 'Madison' on the other. JVW is labeled 'John Bell Williams' on one chart and 'Raymond' on the other. EVERY airport in the U.S.A. should show the same names on ALL charts! AND it should be the one commonly used by the pilots that operate out of that airport. (Whoever came up with the current plan needs to find another job, maybe as a puzzle maker).
ASRSN:2294794.s: A pilot reported that inconsistent airport names between IFR Low Altitude Charts and VFR Sectionals create an ongoing safety danger. The reporter cited examples in the Jackson, MS area where airports like MBO and JVW have different names on each chart, urging standardization to common pilot usage.

ASRSN:2294815.n: Climbout from ZZZ, autopilot did not level at selected 1700 with 'alt capt' displayed on Flight Mode Annunciator (FMA). 3 attempts at autopilot disengagement were required via the trim switch to regain manual control. ATC issued heading/altitude/low altitude alert while significant autopilot mistrim was corrected.Aircraft autopilot had recently been squawked for autopilot failure following repaint at ZZZ1.
ASRSN:2294815.s: During climbout from ZZZ, the autopilot failed to level at 1700 feet despite 'alt capt' on the FMA, requiring three trim switch disengagements to regain manual control. The incident involved significant mistrim correction and followed a recent autopilot failure report after the aircraft's repaint.

ASRSN:2294838.n: My search and rescue drone team was invited to come do a demo of our capabilities at a conference which happened in Location X this year. This was a huge honor for our team to be invited. While there we demonstrated how we use drones like the DJI M30T to search for lost people and our command vehicle. We took along with us our Flycart 30 as well. We did a very short demo of this aircraft taking all safety precautions in mind and we accomplished everything without incident. We feel that the demo was a huge success show teams from across the world the life saving capabilities of these aircraft. I hope that we empowered teams and gave them ideas as to how to implement these tools to their life saving efforts. Now that I am home and rereading our Certificate of Authorization (COA), I see that I didn't comply with the details as our COA only covers operations within our county. This was a complete oversight and I see that I operated that small demo illegally and I should have filed for permission to put on that demo in Class G airspace. I recognize my error, I feel awful for it, and it will not happen again. In the future if such requests come I will file for a waiver to be able to conduct these demos legally.
ASRSN:2294838.s: The pilot operated a DJI M30T and Flycart 30 drone for a search and rescue demo at a conference in Location X without incident. Upon review, the pilot realized the operation violated their Certificate of Authorization, which is limited to their county, resulting in an illegal flight in Class G airspace.

ASRSN:2294839.n: While conducting flight operations at Location X, a lost link event occurred at an altitude of 80 feet AGL in the vicinity of Location X. The ground station was in the vicinity of Location Y. The automatic return to home function safely landed the aircraft without incident.Time line of flight:0:00:00 aircraft motors turned on0:00:05 entered hover0:00:18 maneuvered 15 feet away at an altitude of 10 feet above ground level0:00:26 climbed to 40 feet above ground level0:00:36 performed side slip maneuver 30-35 feet away0:00:40 rotated 90 degrees counterclockwise and began climbing to 80 feet above ground level0:01:11 lost control of aircraft and automatic return to home activated0:01:56 aircraft landed0:02:00 aircraft motors shut off
ASRSN:2294839.s: During flight operations at Location X, a drone lost control at 80 feet AGL due to a lost link event. The aircraft's automatic return to home function activated, resulting in a safe landing without incident.

ASRSN:2294900.n: At end of redeye into IAH we were cleared a visual approach for RWY 27. When selecting to go direct to the FAF in LNAV, VNAV was not selected for a couple of seconds which caused us to be high. In an attempt to stabilize the approach we did a S turn which helped with the approach. Combined with our fatigue we were so focused on making the gates and were high during the approach but were constantly verbally discussing the stabilization gates. At the 500 ft mark we thought that the speed was within 15 kts and it was decreasing at that time. When we parked we received a report that we were 5 kts too fast at the 500 ft mark. During the approach at a low altitude we heard 'Too Low Terrain' but both of us saw the runway, visually confirmed that the runway was in sight and in a safe approach situation, and believed that it was just in reference to the higher descent rate and decided to continue the approach. We then realized with the printout that we landed the airplane in flaps 25 instead of the intended 30. While we both thought that we had flaps 30 selected we hyper-fixated on trying to slow the aircraft down and didn't catch our mistake. The rest of the landing was completed safely and touched down within the touchdown zone with no other issues. We were operating redeye flight LAX-IAH. On downwind we got cleared for the visual approach to runway 27. Once cleared for the visual approach, we proceeded direct to the FAF. VNAV wasn't engaged once we went direct, but was quickly identified as well as being high on the path.We configured the aircraft for landing and decided to perform an S turn to correct for altitude. Once the S turn was completed, we began to overly fixate on our vertical profile and airspeed in relation to the stabilized approach criteria. At 500 feet we were on path and speed.Approaching the runway in visual conditions at a low altitude we got a terrain warning. Given our position over the runway and stable state of the aircraft, we elected to land uneventfully, in the touchdown zone.Once we parked at the gate, we got a print out that said we were 5 knots too fast below 500 feet and landed flaps 25. Discussing the approach in our debrief it was evident fatigue, task saturation and a heightened focused on vertical path and speed led to our mistake of not selecting flaps 30. Our intent was to be safe, stable and fully configured for a flaps 30 landing.
ASRSN:2294900.s: Pilots on a redeye LAX-IAH flight cleared for a visual approach to RWY 27 became high after VNAV disengaged, performed an S-turn, and ignored a terrain warning. Fatigue and task saturation caused them to land with flaps 25 instead of 30 and 5 knots fast at 500 feet, though the touchdown was safe.

ASRSN:2294909.n: While on final approach to runway 27 in VMC conditions and hand flying, we received a very brief sink rate as we crossed the highway. We had been following a A321 on final and where fighting wake turbulence the whole approach. While the approach was fully stabilized and flaps 40 per the pilot bulletin, the approach seemed normal until we did received a very brief sink rate GPWS aural. Also, we encountered some mechanical turbulence and that along with the wake caused the approach to be more challenging then normal. I along while the captain felt it much safer to continue the approach. We landed normally and in the touch down zone with ample safety margins. We were cleared for the RNAV 27 at SAN via radar vectors. The airplane was fully-configured (flaps 40) and we had the landing runway in sight. Passing through 500' we were stabilized and on the VNAV path, the First Officer was hand flying by this point and we both stated that the PAPI was showing 3 white over 1 red. At around 400' the first officer stated that he was going to transition visually to capture the PAPI. As soon as we started adjusting our pitch we began to encounter wake turbulence. The airplane began to sink and the FO added power to arrest the descent rate, we heard a sink rate" call out on the EGPWS as we recovered. We were still on glide path per the PAPI and I could no longer see the parking garage so I elected to continue. We landed in the touchdown zone and taxied to the gate."
ASRSN:2294909.s: The First Officer hand-flew an RNAV 27 approach at SAN in VMC, encountering wake turbulence and mechanical turbulence that caused a brief sink rate and EGPWS aural warning. The crew recovered by adding power, continued the stabilized approach, and landed normally in the touchdown zone.

ASRSN:2294958.n: At the end of the pushback of flight ABCD, the aircraft start moving forward, when the communications person was trying to close the communications panel. The wing walker still with the stop signal in front of the plane, wing walker started making movements towards the Captain, which could have stopped the aircraft and avoid endangering people still near the plane.
ASRSN:2294958.s: During pushback of flight ABCD, the aircraft moved forward while a communications person closed the panel and a wing walker held a stop signal. The wing walker then signaled the Captain to stop, preventing potential injury to personnel near the aircraft.

ASRSN:2294975.n: Qualified Upgrade 4th flight. 2nd landing, 1st landing at night. Normal approach, stable at 1000ft. 500ft Vapp sink 700. We were about 2.5 miles in trail of another aircraft landing the same runway. Crew noticed wake turbulence associated with this. Around 50 ft I noticed a higher than normal sink rate. As I noticed this I moved my hand to the yoke. Around 30 ft I began applying backpressure along with the student. Sink rate slowed. However, there was not enough time to fully arrest the abnormal sink rate. This resulted in what I would describe as a hard landing.Cause: CA IOE first trip, 2nd landing, 1st at night. I believe that after a long day the student initially picked a sight picture that he may have been taught to use in the simulator as a way to not land outside of the touchdown zone. I also believe he may not have corrected his assumptions for night as he had not flown the actual aircraft in multiple weeks. Suggestions: Better situational awareness and use of all available resources. RA callouts, and VSI during landing phase. Stable approach using Autopilot and Autothrottle at night ended with a hard landing. Autopilot disconnected around 500' but Autothrottles were left on. Cause: Night illusion on approach to land, first night landing in the left seat, wake turbulence on landing.Suggestions: I should have stayed slightly above the glide slope knowing that we were coming in behind a mainline aircraft. The crew had experienced about 2 seconds of wake turbulence around 3000' on localizer. With it being my first landing at night while in the left seat, I could have asked the Check Airman to be ready to assist with minor corrections. I was a flight instructor for just over 2years and know full well that night landings are rarely smooth the first few times a student does them due to night illusions and a different sight picture.
ASRSN:2294975.s: A Check Airman and student pilot experienced a hard landing during a night approach in wake turbulence. The reporter attributes the event to night illusions, an incorrect sight picture, and delayed correction of an abnormal sink rate.

ASRSN:2295036.n: On taxi out in ZZZ, aircraft posted HYD 3B caution message. Aircraft was stopped and the QRH was called for. Upon following the steps listed in the QRH, it was discovered that the HYD 3 system fluid levels were low. Turning the 3B pump on during the QRH was also shortly followed by the HYD 3A caution message. The QRH was run for the HYD 3A caution. After finishing the QRH for the HYD3A caution, the HYD3 Low press message posted shortly after. During this process, an attempt was made to vacate the main taxiway and after releasing the parking brake it was also discovered that nose wheel steering had been lost. The brake was set once more and the aircraft was brought into the gate under tow.Cause: Hydraulic 3 system Failure On taxi, HYD 3B caution. QRH followed, low fluid level discovered(10%) followed by HYD 3A caution, QRH looked at, not followed due to low fluid levels. HYD 3 LO PRESS caution, QRH not followed due to fluid levels. Radio to Maintenance, prompted to call Maintenance Control. Upon reaching clearance to taxi somewhere to park and call, nose wheel steering ability lost, brakes promptly applied and set, ramp notified for a tug, towed to gate. (QRH ignored due to calling for turning pumps ON with inadequate fluid levels)Cause: Hydraulic 3 failure
ASRSN:2295036.s: During taxi out, the flight crew encountered a Hydraulic 3 system failure indicated by low fluid levels and multiple caution messages. After losing nose wheel steering while attempting to vacate the taxiway, the aircraft was secured and towed to the gate.

ASRSN:2295037.n: Severe turbulence encounterCause: We were at the top of the clouds at our filed altitude of F300. We elected to climb to F320 for a smoother ride and were cleared there by ATC. Shortly after, it seemed we should climb again to get above the bumps to F340. We contacted ATC, were cleared and started climbing. Between F320 and just below F340, we experienced significant turbulence with large airspeed and attitude deviations, we slowed our rate of climb to avoid any continuation of speed decay. When we were able to, we called the flight attendants to take their seat and they advised that they had just finished their service, that they were ok, and that there were no injuries. Everyone remained in their seats for the duration of the flight, as well as on the return leg which also had considerable turbulence though less severe. Suggestions: None. All of our available resources did not indicate that this would be as significant of a threat.
ASRSN:2295037.s: The flight crew encountered severe turbulence between FL320 and FL340 while climbing above clouds, causing large airspeed and attitude deviations. No injuries occurred, and the crew slowed the climb rate to prevent speed decay while flight attendants secured themselves.

ASRSN:2295062.n: Ramp cleared us for pushback in ZZZ. Once in the ramp at Spot #X on Taxiway 1 short of Taxiway 2, Ramp cleared us to switch over to ground.There was a long taxi delay to runway XXL. Ground advised us to taxi left on [Taxiway] 3 and continue all the way around the airport, to then hold short of Taxiway 4. We did not hear any mention of yielding to other aircraft.As we began our taxi out of the ramp, Aircraft X began crossing Runway XXL and taxiing straight at us opposite direction on 1. The Captain asked if Aircraft X was supposed to yield to us. Before I could answer, he brought the aircraft safely to a stop. Aircraft X didn't yield and turned right onto 3 in front of us. We continued taxiing and the ground frequency was incredibly busy. We contacted ZZZ Clearance and advised them of the situation, inquiring what happened. They stated they would investigate.
ASRSN:2295062.s: The flight crew experienced a taxi conflict at ZZZ airport when Aircraft X failed to yield on Taxiway 1 while crossing Runway XXL. The Captain stopped the aircraft safely, and the crew reported the incident to Clearance, who stated they would investigate.

ASRSN:2295074.n: IP (Flight Instructor) told SP (student pilot) to perform a short fielding landing to the 1,000 footers, full procedure, on runway XX at ZZZ. Touchdown was not abnormally rough, SP began applying brakes immediately. It did not feel like an abnormal amount of brake pressure was being applied. After we began slowing down, the plane began to skid as the tires locked up. Right after the skid began, we felt the tires pop, initially thinking it was only the right main. Advised FBO of the issue over the radio and they were quick to come out with a tow as we were stuck on the runway. After shutting down and getting out, we realized both tires had popped. Plane was towed to the ramp by FBO crew.
ASRSN:2295074.s: A student pilot and flight instructor experienced a runway skid and dual main tire blowouts during a short-field landing at ZZZ. The aircraft became stuck on the runway after the tires locked up and popped, requiring a tow by the FBO crew.

ASRSN:2295214.n: While flying north along the river at or below 500' AGL my engine sputtered and lost power, I made a landing on a gravel bar, the nose wheel was torn off and the front end dropped causing the propeller to strike the ground.
ASRSN:2295214.s: The pilot experienced engine power loss while flying north at or below 500' AGL and made a forced landing on a gravel bar. The nose wheel tore off, causing the front end to drop and the propeller to strike the ground.

ASRSN:2295243.n: While flying in the downwind for Runway 15 at FLY at the pattern altitude of 7900 feet, my student and I experienced a near mid-air collision with Aircraft Y flying in the opposite direction of the downwind at nearly the exact same altitude. The aircraft was not speaking on the airport frequency and proceeded to fly over a helicopter taking off from Runway XX. They did not reply to our attempts to contact them and after some maneuvering, departed the area to the south. We made a right 360 to attempt to contact the aircraft and to warn other local traffic of the hazardous operations of the airplane.
ASRSN:2295243.s: A pilot and student on downwind for Runway 15 at 7,900 feet experienced a near mid-air collision with Aircraft Y flying opposite at the same altitude. The unresponsive aircraft ignored radio calls, flew over a departing helicopter, and departed south, prompting the pilot to perform a 360 to warn local traffic.

ASRSN:2295251.n: At around XA:15 at ZZZ, I was in the process of landing my C208B on RWY XXL after a survey mission. My initial touchdown was standard, with no hard landing or loss of directional control. About 3 seconds after touchdown, I noticed that my right rudder pedal was shaking abnormally. My aircraft continued to slow down but started to veer to the right slightly. I input the necessary controls to avoid a runway excursion. My aircraft eventually came to a full stop, and after increasing some thrust, my aircraft did not move. My aircraft had stopped about 150 feet away from the RWY hold-short lines on [Taxiway] 1. I looked out my right window and noticed that my right main landing gear wheel was flat. The tire did not blow, it was flat. I shut my engine down, notified the tower. After about 5 minutes, airport Ops came to assist along with FBO MX (Maintenance). After about 30-40 minutes, airport ops and MX were successfully able to tug my aircraft off the runway. The runway was reopened without incident. No damage to the aircraft or injuries to POB (Persons on Board).
ASRSN:2295251.s: The pilot of a C208B experienced abnormal right rudder pedal shaking and a flat right main tire shortly after landing on RWY XXL. The pilot maintained directional control to stop safely, and the aircraft was later towed off the runway with no damage or injuries.

ASRSN:2295261.n: On Day 0, an abnormal situation occurred during flight ABCD.Situation:Everything was carried out without anomalies during the initial climb, ATC instructed us to climb and maintain FL270. Our final cruising level was FL370.Once level at FL270, an ECAM CAUTION 'AIR PACK 1 REGUL FAULT' appeared, showing on the ECAM SD BLEED PAGE both PACKS in amber and position CLOSED. I assessed for a few seconds the condition of the PACK FLOW VALVES and verified on the OVERHEAD PANEL if there was any light on the pushbutton switch related to the current system status, I noticed that the information presented did not correspond to the associated ECAM.An OEB (Operations Engineering Bulletin) was mentioned and recalled, and it was discussed between both pilots that the ECAM entry did not correspond to our situation, so a possible application of said OEB was dismissed. As part of my analysis, I verified the status of CAB ALT and CAB V/S, which apparently was increasing at 900 ft/min and a cabin altitude of 5,450 ft.Actions:A few seconds later, ATC instructed us to continue the climb, to which we requested to maintain FL270. I decided to call the flight attendants normally to inform them that we were facing a possible depressurization and that they should remain seated.I determined that for safety we had to descend to 13,000 ft, an altitude previously identified during the threat management phase in the BRIEFING. Initially, descent to FL190 was authorized.During the descent between FL270 and FL190, there was an abrupt increase in CAB V/S and CAB ALT, reaching and exceeding 9,550 ft of CAB ALT, so the EMER DESCENT procedure was applied in accordance with the manual. Priority handling was requested with ATC.ATC instructed us to descend to 13,000 ft and gave an initial heading toward ZZZ, which I identified as meeting minimum obstacle clearance altitudes and confirmed that the AFS (Autoflight System) was complying with the ATC instruction.Once established in descent, the ECAM action lines were initiated.It is important to mention that the CAB ALT showed a positive trend and close to 14,000 ft CAB ALT, so the MASKS MAN ON pushbutton switch was pressed in accordance with manual/EMER DESCENT.Upon reaching 10,000 ft MSL, the First Officer removed his oxygen mask, followed by me.Due to weather conditions, operational benefits, emergency service support, and commercial and Dispatch advantages, the conscious decision was made to return to ZZZ.I told my purser that we were already at 10,000 ft, that everything was under control, and that we were returning to ZZZ with an estimated 15 minutes. In addition to notifying her of those elements, I asked about the passengers' status and added that I would make an announcement regarding what had happened and the next steps.This passenger announcement was made once the decision had been taken, emphasizing the following points:Everything is under control.We are returning to ZZZ.Estimated 15 minutes to landing.Please follow the instructions of our flight attendants.Already flying toward ZZZ, I took into account the crew's well-being. In particular, my First Officer was in good condition to begin the instrument approach to Runway XXL. I decided to transfer controls to prepare the FMGC and ensured that APPROACH C/L had been completed.We noticed that ZZZ Approach expedited other traffic to give us priority, however, I decided to notify them that we were no longer in a priority situation so that we could continue a normal approach and thus manage our workload.During final approach, we received a call from the cabin crew. Given the nature of the situation, I decided to authorize the First Officer to answer it, anticipating a possible medical situation and being in time to make the request to ATC.Medical assistance was requested upon confirming that the call was due to an infant who was unconscious.Result:The landing was carried out without incident.After landing, police services escorted us to gate XX, and upon opening the aircraft door, they entered to ensure everything was under control.A passenger announcement was made prioritizing the following points:Reason for the return.Situation under control at all times.Message of calm.Appreciation for patience and cooperation.
ASRSN:2295261.s: Pilots on flight ABCD experienced a cabin depressurization during climb due to an air pack fault, triggering an emergency descent to 13,000 ft and a return to ZZZ. The aircraft landed safely after an infant became unconscious, requiring medical assistance upon arrival.

ASRSN:2295283.n: I was on break in the bunk when the aircraft entered an area of severe mountain wave. The plane lost approximately 500 feet and the airspeed briefly increased to Vmo plus 10-15 knots. The pilot flying retarded the throttles to idle and extended the speed brakes to reduce airspeed below and then return to altitude. The event lasted approximately 3 minutes before subsiding. The seat belt sign was on and the flight attendants were seated immediately. Fortunately, there were no injuries and we landed in ZZZZ on schedule. During my debriefing with the pilots, they stated that other aircraft in the vicinity reported only airspeed fluctuations but no severe mountain wave or moderate turbulence. Dispatch notified and maintenance write up put into the logbook. We debriefed with the maintenance team in ZZZZ when we landed.
ASRSN:2295283.s: A cabin crew member reported that the aircraft encountered severe mountain waves, causing a 500-foot altitude loss and airspeed exceeding Vmo by 10-15 knots.
